what_it_does: Processing-in-memory (PIM) means building arithmetic units directly inside the DRAM memory chip so that data does not have to travel to and from a distant processor chip for every operation. To program such a chip, you need a small instruction set — a language that tells the in-memory compute units what to do. This paper focuses on a practical bottleneck: even with PIM, two costs remain high — sending the PIM program code from the CPU into the memory chip before it can run, and moving data between the CPU and the memory chip to set up and collect results. The proposed fix adds two new ways to refer to data addresses within the PIM instruction set: indexed addressing (where the address is computed from a register plus a table of offsets) and base-offset addressing (where the address is a register value plus a fixed number). These are standard tricks in conventional CPU instruction sets, but adding them to the PIM instruction set allows the chip to describe complex data layouts in fewer instructions and move less data overall, cutting both the program-loading overhead and the data-transfer overhead.
